q: Does the inplace Y-basis construction extend to non-CSS codes (e.g. color codes, XZZX, Bacon-Shor), or is diagonal twist-defect fusion specifically tied to the rotated-surface CSS structure?
basis: The paper's construction relies on twist defects that live on the standard rotated surface code's XZ boundary structure. Whether an analogous 'inplace' non-braid Y-basis access exists for non-CSS or twisted-CSS codes is not addressed and is not obvious from the construction.
next_steps: Attempt an analogous construction on the color code (Steane hex lattice), which supports transversal H and therefore has a natural Y-basis question; test on XZZX where the noise-biased asymmetry may allow an even shorter inplace path. Metric: does a fused-defect Y patch exist that stays inside the native code footprint and preserves distance?

q: Can the inplace-Y measurement be composed with lattice surgery for direct multi-patch Y-basis parity checks (Y1 tensor Y2 tensor ... measurement) without going through XZ-decomposition?
basis: Lattice surgery is the standard multi-qubit parity primitive but is defined for X-type and Z-type joins on standard patches. A native Y-type join built on top of inplace-Y would eliminate one layer of XZ-decomposition overhead in factory circuits, potentially compounding the per-Y savings.
next_steps: Design a merge protocol between two inplace-Y patches (fuse two twist-defect regions across a shared boundary), simulate the merged Y1Y2 parity extraction in stim, and compare LER vs XZ-decomposed baseline (measure X1X2 then Z1Z2, combine) at matched d and p. Look for a spacetime-volume win analogous to the single-patch case.

q: What is the end-to-end savings when inplace-Y is used inside a magic-state distillation factory (e.g. 15-to-1 or 116-to-12) vs the standard Y-via-distillation baseline?
basis: The paper motivates its construction by noting factories consume hundreds of Y-basis measurements per T state, but does not simulate a full factory. The per-Y saving multiplies but the actual factor depends on decoder-correlations across many nearby Y measurements, which the paper does not exercise.
next_steps: Compose the released Y-basis circuit into a 15-to-1 factory circuit (Litinski's compact layout), sample end-to-end with pymatching or sinter's correlated matching, and compare (a) T-state error rate vs the standard braid or distillation baseline at matched physical p, (b) qubit-round volume. Free-endpoint compatible.

q: How does the inplace-Y logical-error-rate scale under biased noise (Z-biased, e.g. bias eta = 100 or 1000) rather than SI1000-depolarizing?
basis: The inplace construction concentrates twist defects along a diagonal, which is a locally denser region. Under biased noise, the effective distance for the biased Pauli can be very different from the depolarizing distance; whether inplace-Y retains or loses its efficiency advantage under bias is not addressed by the paper.
next_steps: Rebuild the released .stim circuits with a biased-depolarizing noise channel (parameter eta) applied to the same locations, sample LER at bias in {1, 10, 100, 1000} for d in {5, 7, 9}, and check whether the inplace-vs-braid relative advantage is preserved or inverted. Stim + pymatching handle this natively.

q: Which superconducting and neutral-atom hardware platforms can execute the diagonal twist-defect fusion natively, and what is the actual physical-qubit and native-gate overhead once platform connectivity and gate set are honored?
basis: The construction assumes ideal square connectivity and unrestricted CX/CZ scheduling. Google's Willow-class chips have this; Rigetti, IBM heavy-hex, IonQ chain, and neutral-atom rearrangement-based systems do not. The diagonal fusion pattern may or may not compile efficiently onto those.
next_steps: Take the released Y-basis .stim circuit, run a naive SWAP-network compilation onto (i) heavy-hex, (ii) linear-nearest-neighbor, (iii) neutral-atom rearrangeable connectivity, measure the depth and two-qubit gate blow-up factor, and re-simulate LER with the corresponding platform-specific noise model. Compare against a naive XZ-round-trip baseline compiled onto the same connectivity to see whether the inplace advantage survives real hardware constraints.
